items.q: OTT describes how video is delivered over the internet, while CTV describes the TV screen it is watched on.
items.why: OTT is the delivery method. CTV is the connected device. A streaming show on a phone is OTT but not CTV.

items.q: Most CTV ads can be skipped after five seconds, just like many online video ads.
items.why: Many CTV ads play as full, non-skippable spots, which is one reason completion rates are high.

items.q: SSAI makes ads harder for ad blockers to stop, because the ad is stitched into the video stream.
items.why: The ad arrives from the same server as the show, so the player cannot easily tell them apart.

items.q: Server-side ad insertion always gives the buyer the same device detail as client-side insertion.
items.why: With SSAI some device signals can be lost, so extra steps are often needed to pass them on for measurement.

items.q: A FAST channel is free for the viewer and paid for by advertising.
items.why: FAST means free ad-supported streaming TV. It looks like a linear channel but arrives over the internet.

items.q: AVOD, SVOD and TVOD describe how a streaming service earns its money.
items.why: Ad-supported, subscription and pay-per-title are three different business models.

items.q: Household targeting means an ad is chosen for one named person on the sofa.
items.why: It targets a home, so whoever is watching, including several people, sees the same ad.

items.q: On a shared TV, more than one person may watch the same ad, which is called co-viewing.
items.why: It makes counting people more difficult than counting devices or households.

items.q: Competitive separation tries to keep rival brands out of the same ad pod.
items.why: A car brand usually does not want its competitor in the very next ad slot.

items.q: Because CTV ads are shown on big screens, they work the same way as banner ads on a phone.
items.why: The screen, the viewing situation and the way viewers respond are different, so the measures are too.
